title: Anchoring thread without a knot
subtitle: Loop start, away knot, and waste knot: three clean thread starts for counted needlework.
excerpt: A knot on the back of a needlework piece bulks under the cloth, shifts with washing, and pushes through to the front. Three no-knot methods anchor thread cleanly for the first few stitches until the working thread holds itself.
sourceNotes:
Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Thread starting methods for embroidery.
Weldon's Practical Needlework, volume 1 (1886), Internet Archive. Loop and knot starting methods.
Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), Internet Archive. Anchoring and knot techniques.

glossaryTerms.definition: A knotless start for two or any even number of strands: fold one strand in half, thread the cut ends, and catch the folded loop under the first stitch on the back.

A temporary knot placed on the front of the cloth at least 5 cm from the first stitch. The working stitches travel over the tail on the back, anchoring it. Once anchored, the knot is snipped off the front and the tail trimmed.

A knot placed in the seam allowance or border margin of the cloth, outside the stitching area, so the thread tail runs under the back of the cloth to the start position. The knot is cut away after the tail is secured.

content.text: A knot on the back of a piece shifts under the cloth as it is washed and pressed, eventually showing through the front as a bump. Embroiderers anchor thread three other ways, each suited to a different situation. All three let you start stitching immediately; the tail is secured by the first few stitches rather than by a knot.

items.name: Stranded cotton, separated to working count

content.text: works for any even strand count (two, four, or six strands). Cut one strand at double your working length, fold it in half, and thread both cut ends through the needle. Begin the first stitch as normal, but on the return pass, send the needle through the folded loop on the back of the cloth. Pull firm. The loop grips the thread.

works for any strand count, including single-strand work where the loop start doesn't apply. Tie a small knot at the end of the thread, then send the needle down through the front of the cloth about 5 cm in the direction you'll be stitching. Come up at the start position and begin. Each stitch passes over the tail on the back and anchors it. After three or four stitches, snip the knot off the front and pull the short tail to the back, then run it under the worked stitches and trim.

sits outside the stitching area entirely. Knot the thread and push it through the cloth from the front in the seam allowance or blank margin. The thread runs under the cloth to the stitching area and is anchored as you stitch. Trim the knot off once the tail is covered.

attrs.heading: What goes wrong
attrs.intro: Problems that appear when anchoring methods are applied wrongly.

items.symptom: The loop start slips after a few stitches
items.cause: The needle didn't pass through the folded loop on the back at the first stitch.
items.fix: Pull the thread out and start again. Make sure the needle goes through the loop, not beside it.

items.symptom: The away knot leaves a hole on the front
items.cause: The knot was placed too close to the working area and was snipped too early.
items.fix: Place the knot at least 5 cm from the first stitch and wait until at least four stitches are worked before snipping.

items.symptom: A thread bump shows through on the front
items.cause: A conventional knot was used on the back of the cloth.
items.fix: On the next piece, switch to one of the three no-knot methods. On an existing piece, carefully undo the first few stitches, remove the thread, and restart cleanly.

content.text: All three anchoring methods are used across every counted-thread discipline. The
habit produces a flatter back and a cleaner finish when the piece is mounted or pressed.
